meta.title: Who really said "Me Tarzan, you Jane"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: The 1932 film never says it. On screen Tarzan just points and repeats two names. The catchphrase came from Johnny Weissmuller joking that he was no actor.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Me Tarzan, you Jane'?
meta.ogDescription: Tarzan the Ape Man never contains the line. On screen Tarzan says only "Jane. Tarzan." with pointing — the catchphrase was Weissmuller's own joke to Photoplay.

answer.label: Not quite — on screen it is only “Jane. Tarzan.”
answer.authorDates: 1893–1951 · Welsh composer and actor; credited with the dialogue for Tarzan the Ape Man (1932)
answer.sourceLine: In Tarzan the Ape Man (Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, 1932) Tarzan’s side of the famous exchange is nothing but the two proper nouns: Jane offers “I’m Jane Parker. Understand? Jane,” then points at him — “And you? You?” — and Tarzan answers by pointing at her and at himself — “Jane. Tarzan. Jane. Tarzan…” — faster and faster. The pidgin sentence “Me Tarzan, you Jane” is nowhere in the picture; the earliest printing of it we could find is Johnny Weissmuller’s own joke to Photoplay in June 1932, two months after the film opened.

source.heading: The scene, as actually written

docMeta.dd: 2 April 1932 · Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, directed by W. S. Van Dyke
Cyril Hume (adaptation) and Ivor Novello (dialogue), from characters created by Edgar Rice Burroughs
Tarzan (Johnny Weissmuller) and Jane Parker (Maureen O’Sullivan) — fictional characters

source.excerpt:
Jane: I’m Jane Parker. Understand? Jane. [pointing to herself] Jane.
Tarzan [touching her]: Jane.
Jane [pointing to Tarzan]: And you? You?
Tarzan [touching his chest]: Tarzan. Tarzan.
Jane: Tarzan.
Tarzan: Jane. Tarzan. Jane. Tarzan. Jane. Tarzan. Jane. Tarzan. Jane…
trail: Wikiquote’s page for Tarzan the Ape Man (1932 film) ↗ transcribes two dialogue passages from the picture. Neither is the line everybody quotes — and neither is even the name-exchange scene, which Wikiquote does not print at all.

The Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, quoted in a footnote to Wikipedia’s Ivor Novello ↗ article, says Novello “reputedly originated the line that gave rise to the now mythical if inaccurate ‘Me Tarzan. You Jane’ (originally – with appropriate pointing – ‘Tarzan. Jane.’)”. Note the ODNB’s own hedge: reputedly.

Three separate transcriptions of the scene agree. Ross Petras’s Stupid Movie Lines ↗ prints Jane’s cue and Tarzan’s reply as the two names alternating; Diane Giddis and Paul Kirchner print the same run of names, Giddis adding the stage direction “pointing to her and himself.”

The phrase itself surfaces in Photoplay for June 1932 ↗ — but out of Weissmuller’s mouth, not Tarzan’s: “You see, I’m no actor. Well, I didn’t have to act in ‘Tarzan, the Ape Man’ — just said, ‘Me Tarzan, you Jane.’” Across the Media History Digital Library’s searchable fan and trade press, an exact-phrase search returns ten printings, and this is the earliest of them.
source.excerptNote: Assembled from three independent published transcriptions that agree on both the wording and the pointing — Ross Petras’s Stupid Movie Lines ↗, Diane Giddis’s The Movie Dialogue Quiz Book and Paul Kirchner’s Everything You Know Is Wrong, all searchable in full text through the Internet Archive. Jane’s intervening cue — “And you? You?” — is restored from the fuller transcription in Wikipedia’s List of film misquotes ↗, cited there to The New York Times; none of the three books prints it. No transcription contains the sentence “Me Tarzan, you Jane” — Tarzan’s own lines are nothing but the two names.

source.rightsNote: Tarzan the Ape Man was registered for US copyright by Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Distributing Corp. on 14 March 1932 (registration LP2913) and released on 2 April 1932, per the AFI Catalog ↗. US public domain currently reaches works published through 1930, so a 1932 studio release sits well inside copyright — and because screen writing is work for hire, the rights belong to the studio rather than to Novello or Hume.

author.name: Ivor Novello
author.kicker: The writer of the real line
author.heading: Ivor Novello
author.metaLine: 1893–1951 · Welsh composer, actor and dramatist; dialogue credit on Tarzan the Ape Man (1932)
author.bio: Ivor Novello — born David Ivor Davies in Cardiff — was one of the biggest British entertainers of the first half of the twentieth century: a matinee idol who played the title role in Hitchcock’s The Lodger, and the composer, at twenty-one, of “Keep the Home Fires Burning,” the song that defined the British home front in the First World War. An MGM contract took him to Hollywood in the early 1930s and gave him strikingly little to do; writing the dialogue for Tarzan the Ape Man was essentially the sum of it, after which he returned to London and produced the string of hit musicals he is actually remembered for. The Ivor Novello Awards, named for him in 1955, still carry his name through British songwriting.

misattribution.heading: What actually happened
misattribution.intro: Nobody here is falsely credited — the film is real, the scene is real, and it is one of the most watched moments in early sound cinema. What went wrong is the grammar. Three different things get collapsed into one remembered sentence:

items.why: The picture contains no line resembling “Me Tarzan, you Jane.” Tarzan’s side of the exchange is built entirely out of two proper nouns and a pointing finger, which is precisely what makes it work: a man who has no grammar yet reaching for the only two words he needs. Wikiquote’s transcription of the film ↗ carries no such line.

Burroughs’s Tarzan is literate. He teaches himself to read from picture books and writes Jane courtly full sentences — “I am Tarzan of the Apes. I want you. I am yours. You are mine… You are Jane Porter, I saw it in your letter” — in Tarzan of the Apes ↗. The monosyllabic jungle man is MGM’s invention, not Burroughs’s; the string “you Jane” appears nowhere in the novel.

The catchphrase came from the star himself, in a Photoplay interview published in June 1932 ↗, deprecating his own performance: “I should stick to Tarzan … You see, I’m no actor. Well, I didn’t have to act in ‘Tarzan, the Ape Man’ — just said, ‘Me Tarzan, you Jane.’ I’ll never be able to act.” Whether he minted the joke or repeated one already going round the lot cannot be settled from the page — but the print record starts with him, not with the screen.

misattribution.truthLine: So the line people quote is a real quotation by a real person — it is just not a line from the film, and Weissmuller was mocking the role rather than playing it. The words the film’s audience actually heard were written for the screen by Ivor Novello, who took the dialogue credit on the picture per the AFI Catalog ↗, working over Cyril Hume’s adaptation.

context.heading: Why the film had to invent a Tarzan who couldn’t talk
lead: MGM’s difficulty in 1931 was that the Tarzan of the books talks perfectly well. Burroughs had given him a self-taught literacy and a rather formal turn of phrase, which is charming on the page and useless in a talking picture built around a champion swimmer with no acting experience. So the studio took the vocabulary away. What Novello and Hume left Weissmuller was close to nothing — and out of that nothing came the scene everyone remembers, in which two people who share no language establish the only two words that matter.

It is a genuinely good piece of writing, and it is entirely nouns. What the culture carried away instead was a grammatical joke that nobody in the film ever makes — and the man who made it was the one complaining he had not been given anything to say.
detailsBody: Hollywood was not a happy posting for Ivor Novello. He arrived on an MGM contract off the back of a Broadway success and, by his biographers’ account, found almost nothing to do there; the dialogue for Tarzan the Ape Man was effectively the whole of it. He went home to London, wrote Glamorous Night and the run of musicals that made him one of the dominant figures in British theatre, and is remembered today for those and for “Keep the Home Fires Burning” — not for the four or five syllables of jungle dialogue that became the most quoted thing he never quite wrote.

The phrase went on to have a long afterlife in exactly the register Weissmuller pitched it in. The Media History Digital Library’s searchable press turns it up as shorthand for crude dialogue in Hollywood magazine in 1937, in Variety in 1952 and again in 1959, and in Motion Picture Daily in 1959 reporting that a new producer had discarded “Me Tarzan, you Jane” dialogue altogether. In every one of those printings it is a stick to beat the films with — never a quotation from them.
context.pull: You see, I’m no actor. Well, I didn’t have to act in ‘Tarzan, the Ape Man’ — just said, ‘Me Tarzan, you Jane.’

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's page for Tarzan the Ape Man (1932 film) transcribes two dialogue passages, neither of which contains 'Me Tarzan, you Jane' or the words 'me'/'you' in that construction. It also credits the film to W. S. Van Dyke and Cyril Hume, based on Burroughs's novel.

The AFI Catalog credits table lists WRITERS: Cyril Hume 'Adpt' (adaptation) and Ivor Novello 'Dial' (dialogue); Director W. S. Van Dyke; Production Company Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Corp. (Loew's, Inc.); Release Date 2 April 1932; Copyright claimant Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Distributing Corp., 14 March 1932, registration LP2913; and gives Weissmuller's dates as 1904-1984. The record contains no mention of 'Me Tarzan, you Jane'.

The OCR text of this Photoplay (June 1932) page literally reads: "I should stick to Tarzan," he explains. "You see, I'm no actor. Well, I didn't have to act in 'Tarzan, the Ape Man' — just said, 'Me Tarzan, you Jane.' I'll never be able to act." — the speaker throughout the piece being Johnny Weissmuller. Adjacent leaves carry the running head 'Photoplay Magazine for June, 1932'.

Wikipedia's Ivor Novello article states he found little to do in Hollywood beyond writing the dialogue for Tarzan the Ape Man, with a footnote quoting the ODNB: 'he reputedly originated the line that gave rise to the now mythical if inaccurate "Me Tarzan. You Jane" (originally – with appropriate pointing – "Tarzan. Jane.")'. It also gives his dates as 15 January 1893 – 6 March 1951 and his birth name as David Ivor Davies.

The full text of Burroughs's Tarzan of the Apes contains zero occurrences of 'you Jane' and no instance of 'Me Tarzan' (the three 'me tarzan' string matches are false positives across word boundaries such as 'time Tarzan' and 'came Tarzan'). It does contain Tarzan writing literate full sentences: 'I am Tarzan of the Apes. I want you. I am yours. You are mine... You are Jane Porter, I saw it in your letter.'

An exact-phrase full-text search of the Media History Digital Library for 'me tarzan, you jane' returns 10 printings across the whole corpus; the earliest is Photoplay (Jan-Jun 1932), and the next earliest is Hollywood (1937). Later hits include Variety (March 1952), Variety (June 1959) and Motion Picture Daily (Apr-Jun 1959, reporting that producer Weintraub had discarded 'Me Tarzan, you Jane' dialogue).

Internet Archive / Open Library full-text search returns the exact string 'Jane. Tarzan. Jane. Tarzan.' from Ross Petras's Stupid Movie Lines and from Diane Giddis's The Movie Dialogue Quiz Book (the latter with the stage direction 'pointing to her and himself'), and returns from Petras the setup line 'Jane: I'm Jane Parker. Understand? Jane. [pointing to herself] Jane. Tarzan (touching her):' plus 'chest): Tarzan. Tarzan. Jane: Tarzan. Tarzan: Jane. Tarzan. Jane. Tarzan...'. It also returns from Frank Hammond Tucker's The Frontier Spirit and Progress: 'The actual dialogue was simply "Tarzan — Jane," supplemented with pointing', and from Paul Kirchner's Everything You Know Is Wrong the same run of alternating names.
The scanned copy of Ross Petras's Stupid Movie Lines indexed by the above full-text search is available at this Internet Archive item.

Quote Investigator has no article investigating 'Me Tarzan, you Jane' — a site search for 'Tarzan' returns only two unrelated articles (the 'fish without a bicycle' and 'I never saw anyone hit with his face' pages), so there is no QI anchor finding to defer to on this quote.

Wikipedia's article on the film gives the release as a 1932 pre-Code MGM production, loosely based on Burroughs' 1912 novel Tarzan of the Apes, 'with the dialogue written by Ivor Novello', directed by W. S. Van Dyke, produced by Irving Thalberg, starring Johnny Weissmuller and Maureen O'Sullivan as Jane Parker. The article never mentions 'Me Tarzan, you Jane'.

Wikipedia's List of film misquotes gives a fuller transcription of the scene than the three books do, including Jane's intervening cue: 'Jane Parker [pointing to herself]: Jane. / Tarzan: Jane. / Jane [pointing to Tarzan]: And you? You? / Tarzan: Tarzan, Tarzan. / Jane: Tarzan! / Tarzan [pointing first to Jane, then to himself]: Jane. Tarzan. Jane. Tarzan. Jane. Tarzan. ...' — cited there to Justin Thomas Kay, 'Movie Misquotations', The New York Times, 15 January 2010. Verified in the raw wikitext.

archive.org/metadata/stupidmovielines0000petr returns access-restricted-item 'true', no lending status, and collections ['internetarchivebooks','printdisabled'] — not 'inlibrary', so the Petras scan is search-inside only and not borrowable. The Kirchner item everythingyoukno0000kirc, by contrast, carries collections ['internetarchivebooks','inlibrary','printdisabled'] and so is borrowable.
